tier_reason: The paper is peer-reviewed (EuroSys 2012). Its Figure 13 measures Masstree against Redis 2.4.5 and memcached 1.4.8 on the same 16 cores. It is not A: the code is public (kohler/masstree-beta: mtd.cc, mtclient.cc) and the CPU model (AMD Opteron 8431) is stated, but the paper gives no compiler or flags.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Figure 13 of the EuroSys'12 paper, in millions of req/s on 16 cores. Uniform get: Masstree 9.10 vs Redis 5.97 (65.6%, ~1.5x derived from page data). Uniform put: 5.84 vs 2.97 (50.9%, ~2.0x derived). MYCSB-C all-get: 9.86 vs Redis 2.70 (27.4%, ~3.65x derived) and vs memcached 5.28 (53.6%, ~1.87x derived). MYCSB-A and MYCSB-B vs Redis: 6.05 vs 2.13 and 8.90 vs 2.69 (~2.8x and ~3.3x derived). The paper says Masstree 'outperforms the other systems on almost all workloads, usually by a substantial margin', giving 'up to 3.7x the throughput' of Redis and memcached on non-uniform workloads. memcached is 7.4% faster on uniform get (9.78 vs 9.10).
corrections.workload: Database of 20M key-value pairs on 16 cores, with logging and network I/O included (25 client machines over 10GbE). Two workload sets: (1) uniform get/put with 1-to-10-byte decimal keys and one 8-byte column, run for 60 s; (2) YCSB-derived MYCSB-A/B/C/E with Zipfian key popularity, 5-to-24-byte keys and ten 4-byte columns. Baselines are 16 Redis 2.4.5 processes and 16 memcached 1.4.8 processes.
corrections.hardware: 48-core server with eight 2.4 GHz six-core AMD Opteron 8431 chips, Linux 3.1.5. Tests use 16 cores on up to three chips; the other cores are disabled.
corrections.license: MIT plus two clauses taken from the W3C license (no use of the copyright holders' names in publicity without prior written permission; title to copyright stays with the holders). It is a custom text, not a verbatim OSI/SPDX license; GitHub reports NOASSERTION.
corrections.caveats: All numbers come from the authors' own EuroSys 2012 paper ('Cache Craftiness for Fast Multicore Key-Value Storage', Mao/Kohler/Morris), not from an independent third party. The paper itself says the system comparisons are 'not entirely fair'. The baselines are 2011-era Redis 2.4.5 and memcached 1.4.8, both hash tables, run as 16 partitioned processes. memcached beats Masstree by 7.4% on uniform gets. The hardware is 2012-era AMD Opteron, and the paper gives no compiler or flags. The LICENSE file is MIT plus W3C-style publicity and title clauses, a custom non-OSI text, so usability stays 'reference'. There have been no commits since 2023-10-12.

notes: Every Figure 13 number in the record matches the paper; the only change was marking the ratios as derived. The record said there was no license file, but a LICENSE file exists with MIT plus W3C-style clauses. It is not verbatim OSI, so usability stays 'reference'; the orchestrator may treat it as effectively permissive. The last commit, 2023-10-12, is about 2.9 years old, so the entry is stale, which the record already said.

tier_reason: These are first-party results. The code is public: dgraph-io/dgraph-benchmarks cachebench/ristretto (cache.go 'base-mutex' = golang/groupcache/lru wrapped in a sync.Mutex) and cachebench/cache_bench_test.go. The blog states the CPU (Intel Core i7-8700K), but neither the blog nor the README gives the Go version or build flags. That makes it the project's own benchmark with partial methodology, which is C.

corrections.baseline: The groupcache LRU (golang/groupcache/lru behind a sync.Mutex). The charts label it 'groupcache'; it is presumably the suite's 'base-mutex' entry.
corrections.claimed_speedup: Approximate values read off the README charts (derived from page data). The SVG axes are labeled; the text is drawn as outlines. Mixed workload (25% writes, 75% reads): Ristretto ~60M ops/s vs groupcache ~20M at 16 goroutines, and ~57M vs ~18M at 64 (~3x). At 4 goroutines it is ~22.6M vs ~11M, and freecache (~25.6M) beats Ristretto there. Read (Zipfian): ~64.5M vs ~19.8M at 64 goroutines (~3.3x). Write (Zipfian): ~53.5M vs ~16.2M at 64 goroutines (~3.3x); fastcache beats Ristretto at 4-12 goroutines. Hit ratio, Search ARC-S3: 48% vs groupcache 23% at 500k capacity and 68% vs 57% at 800k (optimal ~72%). Hit ratio, Database ARC-DS1: 44% vs 21% at 5M and 55% vs 43% at 8M, but goburrow beats Ristretto at 3M and 6-8M. The blog says Ristretto 'suffers in comparison to the others' on the CODASYL trace.
corrections.hardware: Intel Core i7-8700K (3.7 GHz), 16 GB RAM. The Ristretto blog post states this for its throughput runs; the README charts, added 2020-06-29, are not confirmed to come from the same run.
corrections.workload: Concurrent throughput in the dgraph-io/dgraph-benchmarks cachebench suite at 4-64 goroutines: Mixed (25% writes, 75% reads), Read (100% Zipfian) and Write (100% Zipfian). Hit ratios on the ARC-S3 search, ARC-DS1 database, LIRS-GLI looping and ARC-OLTP CODASYL traces. Compared against the groupcache LRU with a mutex, BigCache, FreeCache, FastCache and goburrow/cache, plus a clairvoyant 'optimal' policy on the hit-ratio charts.
corrections.caveats: This is the project's own benchmark suite (dgraph-io/dgraph-benchmarks cachebench), so it stays at Tier C. The CPU (i7-8700K) is stated only in the 2019 blog post, and nothing gives the Go version or build flags. The only numbers are chart images: the README SVGs date from 2020 and the blog charts from 2019. Ristretto is not the fastest everywhere: freecache wins the Mixed workload at 4 goroutines and fastcache wins writes at 4-12. Its hit ratio is not best on every trace either: goburrow is higher on the Database trace at several capacities, and Ristretto is weak on CODASYL. The blog.dgraph.io URL is dead, but the post is mirrored at discuss.dgraph.io/t/5102, which the README links.

notes: The record said the charts were unlabeled; the SVGs render with full axes, legends and values, so approximate numbers were read off them. The original benchmark_url (dgraph-benchmarks cachebench/ristretto) holds only code plus a Ristretto-only example output, so benchmark_url now points to the README charts. Metadata was confirmed: Apache-2.0, 6,994 stars, last commit 2026-09-21, not a fork, not archived.

tier_reason: This is a first-party page. The benchmark code is public (fireducks-dev/polars-tpch, branch fireducks_20250204, a fork of pola-rs/polars-benchmark with pandas queries written by the FireDucks team) and the CPU is stated. It is not A: there is no compiler or flags (FireDucks ships as binary wheels only), library versions for the TPC-H run are unpinned, and a 141x gain with flags unstated triggers the >50x cap. No independent or peer-reviewed source exists, so it is C.

corrections.caveats: All results are first-party (FireDucks' own docs site), and the TPC-H pandas queries were written by the FireDucks team. The db-benchmark result the page cites is FireDucks' own run of the suite (fireducks-dev.github.io/db-benchmark); the official duckdblabs/db-benchmark has no fireducks solution. FireDucks is closed source: PyPI carries only binary wheels (658 wheel files, no sdist), and the GitHub repo holds just a README and notebooks as an issue tracker. That is why usability is 'reference' even though the README and PyPI classifier say 3-Clause BSD. The page gives no pandas/Polars/DuckDB versions for the TPC-H run, and the README installs them unpinned with 'pip install -U'. Including I/O, DuckDB (61x) beats FireDucks (55x). The GitHub repo's last push was 2025-05-22, but PyPI release 1.4.4 shipped 2025-12-02, so maintenance is judged 'active' from releases.

notes: The 141x/55x (FireDucks), 109x/61x (DuckDB) and 58x/50x (Polars) numbers and the m7i.8xlarge / Xeon Gold 6526Y setup all match the page. Tier drops from A to C: the page is first-party, no compiler or flags are possible for a binary-only product, versions are unpinned, and the >50x cap applies. maintenance_status was changed to active because the last PyPI release (2025-12-02) is under 12 months old, even though the issue-tracker repo's last commit is 2025-05-22. The orchestrator may prefer to keep 'stale' by the strict last-commit rule.
